scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I need to figure out whether the sister's decision to refuse her brother's request to borrow her vacation money is morally acceptable. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the sister is 21, in her third year of university, working to pay for her education, and saving for a post-graduation vacation. She's managed to save $2800 so far. Her brother is 30, living with their parents, working a job he's trying to get out of, and is back in school. He's been living with them for 1.5 years. He's been hinting that he needs a vacation and has asked her to borrow her money to go to Japan this summer or fall.

The sister refused because she's concerned her brother is bad with money. She points out that despite earning about the same as her, he's always broke. She doesn't pay rent, which allows her to save, but she does buy her own groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, and uni fees. Her brother doesn't pay rent either, but he doesn't buy groceries, so he's not contributing much beyond that.

The brother is upset, arguing that it's unfair because as the youngest, she got to go on more trips with their parents, while he had to go to college or work. He also says she knew what she wanted for university from the start, whereas he had to go back. He claims she's been spoiled by their parents, which she disagrees with, attributing her financial skills to her father and her university classes.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for the sister to refuse her brother's request?

I think the key points here are:

1. The sister has been saving for her own future vacation, which she's planning to take after graduation in two years. She's worked hard to accumulate this money, especially considering she's paying for her own university and other expenses.

2. The brother has a history of being irresponsible with money. Despite earning a similar amount, he's always broke. He's also in a situation where he's back in school and living with his parents, which might indicate some dependency.

3. The parents have already helped the brother financially, so he's not asking them for more. Instead, he's targeting his sister's savings.

4. The sister is worried about her brother's ability to pay her back, which is a valid concern. If he's bad with money, it's possible he might not be able to repay the loan, leaving her without her vacation money.

5. The brother's arguments about fairness seem to stem from past experiences, but the sister's current situation is different. She's making her own way through university, saving money, and planning for her future.

Considering all this, the sister's decision to refuse the loan seems justified. She's prioritizing her own financial goals and future, and she's rightfully concerned about her brother's ability to repay. It's not unreasonable for her to protect her savings, especially since she's the one who's been responsible with her money.

Additionally, the brother's resentment might be more about his own situation rather than the sister's. He's in a tough spot, but that doesn't necessarily mean the sister is obligated to help him financially, especially when she's already contributing by living with her parents and not paying rent.

So, in conclusion, the sister's action is morally acceptable because she's protecting her own future and has valid concerns about her brother's financial reliability.
